name: Caffeine
lethalBasis: human estimate (about 150-200 mg/kg reported)
notes: The FDA puts toxic effects (racing heart, dangerous heart rhythms, seizures) at roughly 1.2 g, and life-threatening doses typically at 10 to 14 g, though less can be dangerous for children and sensitive people. Pure caffeine powder is far more dangerous than drinks: one teaspoon equals roughly 28 cups of coffee, and it is almost impossible to measure safely at home.

name: Table salt (sodium chloride)
lethalBasis: low end of the reported human range (0.5-1 g/kg)
notes: The daily guidance of 2,300 mg is for sodium, which equals about 5.75 g of salt (a bit under one teaspoon). Salt poisoning is a real risk, especially in small children. Never use salt water to induce vomiting. No firm threshold for toxic effects is shown because published figures vary too widely.

toxicNote: No reliable human dose threshold. Early signs are strong thirst, weakness and nausea; severe cases bring confusion, muscle twitching and seizures.

name: Alcohol (ethanol)
lethalBasis: human estimate; tolerance varies enormously
notes: Around 0.8 g/kg (3 to 4 drinks) brings a blood alcohol level of about 0.10, and severe symptoms can develop at 0.8 to 1.2 g/kg. Drinking fast can be dangerous at far lower amounts, and children are much more vulnerable. US guidance is up to 1 drink a day for women and 2 for men. Signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, passing out. Call 911.

notes: Normal cooking amounts are fine. Poisoning has been reported at about 5 g (roughly 2 teaspoons): nausea, racing heart, confusion, hallucinations, lasting a day or longer. Fatalities are very rare and no lethal dose is established.

name: Sugar (sucrose)
lethalBasis: rat LD50; not a realistic human figure
notes: The lethal figure comes from rats. A person could not realistically eat that much, and the real harms of sugar are long-term, not a single-dose poisoning. The guidance limit is the American Heart Association figure for added sugar for most women and children over 2 (36 g for most men).

toxicNote: Not acutely toxic to people at realistic amounts. Rats given huge doses showed sluggishness and diarrhea. The harm from sugar is long-term, not from a single dose.

name: Acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol)
notes: The Extra Strength label limit is 6 tablets (3,000 mg) in 24 hours; other products have different limits, so check your label. Accidental overdose is common because acetaminophen is hidden in many cold, flu and sleep products. Count every source. An overdose can feel fine for the first day while liver damage develops, so call Poison Control immediately if more than directed was taken.

safeNote: This app does not give a safe daily amount for nicotine from tobacco or vapes. For quit-smoking products, follow the label (see Nicotine gum).
toxicNote: In reported cases, swallowing tobacco or nicotine gum at doses up to about 6 mg per kg caused poisoning symptoms without death. A smaller body gets a bigger dose per kg, so a swallow an adult might shrug off can poison a child.
lethalNote: The widely repeated adult fatal dose of 30 to 60 mg (about 0.5 to 1 mg per kg) traces back to dubious 19th-century self-experiments. A 2014 review in Archives of Toxicology estimates an oral LD50 of about 6.5 to 13 mg per kg instead, and notes people have survived far larger amounts. That is one toxicologist's estimate and is still debated, so do not treat it as a safe margin: any swallow, especially of concentrated e-liquid or by a child, is an emergency.
name: Nicotine
servingName: nicotine absorbed from one cigarette (about 2 mg)
notes: Smoking one cigarette takes up about 2 mg of nicotine, according to the same review. Check the label for the nicotine amount in any product. Call Poison Control right away for any swallow.

There is no simple antidote; treatment is intensive supportive care and sometimes a liver transplant. No fatal dose is established; toxicity depends on the plant part, season and the person.

notes: Do not wait for symptoms. Seek help immediately and keep a piece of the mushroom for identification. Look-alikes make wild mushrooms impossible to judge unless you are an expert, and the Western destroying angel is also dangerous. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or use the webPOISONCONTROL online tool, and name the plant exactly.

toxicNote: Poison Control lists autumn crocus as a poisonous plant. This app does not have a sourced dose figure for it.
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established; toxicity depends on the plant part, season and the person.
name: Autumn crocus
notes: Poison Control lists autumn crocus (Colchicum autumnale) as poisonous. If someone eats any, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or use the webPOISONCONTROL online tool, and name the plant exactly.

safeNote: Do not swallow, and never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or toilet bowl cleaners.
toxicNote: Typical household bleach is 4 to 8 percent sodium hypochlorite. One or two mouthfuls usually cause minor mouth and throat irritation, stomach upset and vomiting. Larger amounts or stronger types, such as pool bleach, cause worse symptoms.
lethalNote: Concentrated bleach can cause permanent damage to the stomach and gut and may result in death. No fatal dose is established.
name: Bleach
notes: Mixing bleach with ammonia makes chlorine gas, which can cause choking and serious breathing problems. If swallowed, follow Poison Control's directions; MedlinePlus says to give water or milk right away unless a provider says not to. Call 1-800-222-1222 for any swallow, eye splash or breathing trouble. Poison centers advise never storing bleach in a cup or food container.

safeNote: Not for eating. Keep pods out of sight and reach of children.
toxicNote: Biting into a pod can cause coughing, choking, trouble breathing and coma. The detergent can also irritate the skin and burn the eyes. Pods cause more stomach irritation and more breathing problems and drowsiness than liquid detergent.
lethalNote: Poison Control lists severe vomiting, severe breathing trouble, esophagus burns and coma as possible effects. No fatal dose is established.
name: Laundry pods
notes: Laundry packets are more concentrated than regular detergent. Store them in the closed original container, up high or locked. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away for any swallow or exposure.

safeNote: Not for eating. Keep out of reach of children.
toxicNote: Standard liquid household detergents and soaps rarely cause serious injury if swallowed accidentally, according to MedlinePlus. Single-use pods are more concentrated and more dangerous (see Laundry pods).
lethalNote: No fatal dose is established.
name: Laundry detergent
notes: Never let detergent touch skin for long, do not inhale fumes, and use gloves. If a child swallows some, give a small amount of water or milk, then call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.

safeNote: Never swallow. Keep batteries and any device with a loose battery away from children.
toxicNote: When a battery is swallowed it is impossible to know whether it will pass or get stuck. A coin-shaped battery caught in the esophagus can cause serious burns in as little as two hours, and larger button batteries can burn a hole through the esophagus or cause death.
lethalNote: This is an emergency, not a dose question. Do not wait for symptoms to appear.
name: Button batteries
notes: If anyone swallows a battery of any size, call the National Battery Ingestion Hotline at 1-800-498-8666 (24 hours) or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 immediately, and go to the emergency room. Over 3,500 people a year in the US swallow button batteries. Watch for coughing, drooling, trouble swallowing, refusing to eat or drink, and fever. Tape over discarded button batteries before throwing them away.
